category.title: Arrays & Math
category.description: Array transformations, prefix sums, math, and number theory algorithms.

algorithms.title: Kadane's Algorithm (Maximum Subarray Sum)
algorithms.summary: Finds the contiguous subarray with the maximum sum in a 1D array in linear O(N) time.
explanation: Maintain two variables: `currMax` (sum of current subarray) and `maxSoFar` (global maximum sum).
Iterate through the array. For each element `x`, add it to `currMax`.
If `currMax` becomes negative, reset `currMax = 0` (starting a fresh subarray from next element).
Update `maxSoFar = max(maxSoFar, currMax)` at each step.
To handle all-negative arrays, initialize `maxSoFar` with the first element or negative infinity.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the contiguous sequence of numbers in an array that has the largest combined sum.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When asked for maximum continuous subarray sum or maximum profit window in single-pass array problems.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Financial stock portfolio maximum gain calculation, image processing signal peak detection, genomic sequence alignment scoring.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Reduces brute-force O(N³) or O(N²) nested loops to single linear scan O(N) with O(1) extra space.

codeTemplates.code:
def max_subarray_sum(nums):
    max_so_far = nums[0]
    curr_max = nums[0]
    
    for i in range(1, len(nums)):
        curr_max = max(nums[i], curr_max + nums[i])
        max_so_far = max(max_so_far, curr_max)
        
    return max_so_far

algorithms.title: Dutch National Flag Algorithm (Sort 0s, 1s, 2s)
algorithms.summary: Sorts an array containing only three distinct elements (e.g. 0s, 1s, 2s) in a single pass with O(1) space.
explanation: Maintain three pointers: `low` (boundary for 0s), `mid` (current element scanner), `high` (boundary for 2s).
Initially `low = 0`, `mid = 0`, `high = n - 1`.
Loop while `mid <= high`:
- If `arr[mid] == 0`: swap `arr[low]` & `arr[mid]`, then `low++`, `mid++`.
- If `arr[mid] == 1`: just `mid++`.
- If `arr[mid] == 2`: swap `arr[mid]` & `arr[high]`, then `high--` (do NOT increment mid yet).

traceSteps: Step 1: nums[mid] = 2. Swap nums[mid] and nums[high] (swap 2 & 0). Array = [0, 0, 2, 1, 1, 2], high = 4.
Step 2: nums[mid] = 0. Swap nums[low] and nums[mid] (swap 0 & 0). low = 1, mid = 1. Array = [0, 0, 2, 1, 1, 2].
Step 3: nums[mid] = 0. Swap nums[low] and nums[mid] (swap 0 & 0). low = 2, mid = 2. Array = [0, 0, 2, 1, 1, 2].
Step 4: nums[mid] = 2. Swap nums[mid] and nums[high] (swap 2 & 1). Array = [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2], high = 3.
Step 5: nums[mid] = 1. mid++. mid = 3, low = 2, high = 3. Array = [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2].
Step 6: nums[mid] = 1. mid++. mid = 4 > high (3). Loop terminates.
Result array is sorted in O(N) time with 0 extra memory: [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2].

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Sorts a 3-valued array in-place without using extra counting arrays or multi-pass sorting algorithms.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When an array contains 3 unique key values (e.g. 0/1/2, Red/White/Blue, Low/Medium/High risk tags).
wAnswers.whereUsed: Partitioning elements in QuickSort pivot steps, multi-class classification bucket sorting in memory managers.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Guarantees exact O(N) time with only 3 pointers and zero memory allocation.

algorithms.title: Boyer-Moore Majority Voting Algorithm (Majority Element > N/2)
algorithms.summary: Finds the majority element that appears more than N/2 times in an array in single pass O(N) time and O(1) space.
explanation: Initialize `candidate = None` and `count = 0`.
Iterate through the array. For each element `x`:
- If `count == 0`, set `candidate = x` and `count = 1`.
- Else if `x == candidate`, increment `count++`.
- Else, decrement `count--`.
The remaining `candidate` is guaranteed to be the majority element if one exists.

traceSteps: Candidate = 2. Verification step counts occurrences of 2: 4 times (> 7/2). Verified output: 2.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the element appearing strictly more than 50% of the time in linear time without hash maps.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When finding dominant element in a stream or array with frequency > N/2 or > N/3.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Consensus voting protocols in distributed systems, real-time telemetry anomaly filtering, stream processing.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Replaces Hash Map frequency count O(N) space with O(1) space and 1 linear pass.

algorithms.title: Next Permutation Algorithm (Lexicographical Order)
algorithms.summary: Rearranges numbers into the lexicographically next greater permutation in-place in linear O(N) time.
explanation: Step 1 (Find Break Point): Scan from right to left to find the first index `i` where `nums[i] < nums[i+1]`.
If no such index exists (array is strictly decreasing), reverse the whole array (first permutation).
Step 2 (Find Swap Target): Scan from right to left to find index `j` where `nums[j] > nums[i]`.
Step 3 (Swap): Swap `nums[i]` and `nums[j]`.
Step 4 (Reverse Suffix): Reverse the subarray from index `i+1` to end of array to get the smallest possible tail suffix.

traceSteps: Step 1: Traverse right-to-left to find first dip where nums[i] < nums[i+1]. Dip at index i = 1 (val = 3, since 3 < 5).
Step 2: Traverse right-to-left to find smallest number > nums[1] (3). Index j = 3 (val = 4, since 4 > 3).
Step 3: Swap nums[1] and nums[3] (swap 3 and 4). Array becomes [1, 4, 5, 3, 2].
Step 4: Reverse elements after index 1 (indices 2 to 4: [5, 3, 2] -> [2, 3, 5]).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Generates the next lexicographical permutation of an array in-place without generating all N! permutations.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When asked for next permutation, next lexicographical number sequence, or TSP permutation search.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Combinatorial optimization solvers, permutation generators in C++ `std::next_permutation`, hardware test pattern sequence generator.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Replaces full DFS recursion generation O(N!) with O(N) single-pass in-place swap & reverse.

algorithms.title: Reversal Algorithm for Array Rotation
algorithms.summary: Rotates an array to the right or left by K steps in O(N) time and O(1) extra space using 3 reverse operations.
explanation: Normalize `k = k % n` (in case `k > n`).
To rotate right by K steps:
1. Reverse the entire array `[0...n-1]`.
2. Reverse the first K elements `[0...k-1]`.
3. Reverse the remaining elements `[k...n-1]`.
To rotate left by K steps: Reverse `[0...k-1]`, reverse `[k...n-1]`, then reverse entire array `[0...n-1]`.

traceSteps: Step 2: Reverse first k elements [7, 6, 5] (index 0 to 2) -> [5, 6, 7]. Array = [5, 6, 7, 4, 3, 2, 1].
Step 3: Reverse remaining n-k elements [4, 3, 2, 1] (index 3 to 6) -> [1, 2, 3, 4]. Array = [5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 3, 4].
Rotated array achieved in O(N) time and O(1) space.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Rotates elements in an array by K positions in-place without creating a temporary copy array.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When rotating arrays, cyclic shift operations, or ring buffer offset realignment.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Circular buffer memory management, GUI carousel item shift, CPU cache line rotation.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Achieves O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space compared to naive cyclic shifts taking O(N * K) or O(N) space.

algorithms.title: Merge Overlapping Intervals Algorithm
algorithms.summary: Combines all overlapping intervals in an array of start-end pairs into non-overlapping ranges.
explanation: Sort intervals by start time `intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])`.
Initialize `merged = [intervals[0]]`.
For each interval `[start, end]` in sorted list:
- Get last interval in `merged`: `lastStart, lastEnd = merged[-1]`.
- If `start <= lastEnd` (overlap): merge by updating `merged[-1][1] = max(lastEnd, end)`.
- Else (no overlap): append `[start, end]` to `merged`.

traceSteps: Step 1: Sort intervals by start time -> [[1,3], [2,6], [8,10], [15,18]].
Step 2: Add first interval [1,3] to merged list.
Step 3: Process [2,6]: Start 2 <= Last end 3 -> Overlap! Merge: end = max(3, 6) = 6. Last interval becomes [1,6].
Step 4: Process [8,10]: Start 8 > Last end 6 -> No overlap! Add [8,10] to merged list.
Step 5: Process [15,18]: Start 15 > Last end 10 -> No overlap! Add [15,18] to merged list.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Consolidates overlapping time windows or numerical ranges into minimal disjoint sets.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When given calendar events, meeting rooms, IP range allocations, or line segment overlaps.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Google Calendar meeting clash detection, OS memory segment allocation, network CIDR range aggregation.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Sorting reduces interval comparison complexity from O(N²) to O(N log N) single pass.

algorithms.title: Prefix Sum & Difference Array Technique
algorithms.summary: Precomputes cumulative sum array to perform range sum queries [L, R] in O(1) constant time.
explanation: Precompute `prefix[i] = prefix[i-1] + arr[i]` with `prefix[0] = 0`.
Sum of range `[L, R]` is calculated instantly as `prefix[R + 1] - prefix[L]`.
Difference Array variant: To apply range addition `+V` to `[L, R]`, execute `diff[L] += V` and `diff[R + 1] -= V`. Take prefix sum at the end.

traceSteps: Step 1: Build Prefix Sum array P where P[i] = P[i-1] + nums[i].
Query answered in O(1) time complexity.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Answers multi-range sum queries in O(1) time and applies batch range update operations.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When querying subarray sums repeatedly or applying range updates (e.g. Subarray Sum Equals K, Car Pooling).
wAnswers.whereUsed: 2D Image integral images for face detection (Viola-Jones), audio loudness metering, database range aggregation.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Replaces O(N) range sum loops with O(1) single subtraction operation.

algorithms.title: Maximum Product Subarray (Kadane Variant)
algorithms.summary: Finds contiguous subarray with maximum product in O(N) time by tracking both current minimum and maximum products.
explanation: Since multiplying two negative numbers yields a positive number, a negative number can turn a minimum product into maximum!
Maintain `currMax` and `currMin` initialized to `nums[0]`.
For each element `x` from index 1:
- If `x < 0`: swap `currMax` and `currMin`.
- `currMax = max(x, currMax * x)`.
- `currMin = min(x, currMin * x)`.
- Update global `ans = max(ans, currMax)`.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds contiguous subarray with maximum multiplicative product handling negative numbers & zeros.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When multiplying elements in continuous subarray where negative signs flip product signs.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Compound interest gain optimization, financial risk model product series analysis.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Computes max product in single linear scan O(N) with O(1) space instead of O(N²) nested loops.

codeTemplates.code:
def maxProduct(nums):
    res = max(nums)
    curr_max = curr_min = 1
    for n in nums:
        if n == 0:
            curr_max = curr_min = 1
            continue
        tmp = curr_max * n
        curr_max = max(n * curr_max, n * curr_min, n)
        curr_min = min(tmp, n * curr_min, n)
        res = max(res, curr_max)
    return res

algorithms.title: Count Inversions in Array (Modified Merge Sort)
algorithms.summary: Counts pairs (i, j) such that i < j and arr[i] > arr[j] in O(N log N) time using Divide and Conquer.
explanation: An inversion pair indicates how far an array is from being sorted.
Modify Merge Sort during the `merge(left, right)` step.
When `arr[i] > arr[j]` (where `i` is in left half and `j` is in right half):
- All remaining elements in left half from `i` to `mid` are also greater than `arr[j]`!
- Add `(mid - i + 1)` to `inversion_count`.
Return total sum of inversions from left half, right half, and merge step.

traceSteps: Divide array into left [8, 4] and right [2, 1].
Merge [8] and [4]: 8 > 4 -> Inversion count += 1. Sorted left = [4, 8].
Merge [2] and [1]: 2 > 1 -> Inversion count += 1. Sorted right = [1, 2].
Compare left[0]=4 with right[0]=1: 4 > 1 -> Inversion count += remaining elements in left (2 elements: 4, 8). count = 2 + 2 = 4.
Compare left[0]=4 with right[1]=2: 4 > 2 -> Inversion count += remaining elements in left (2 elements: 4, 8). count = 4 + 2 = 6.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Measures how out-of-order an array is (number of swaps required to sort).
wAnswers.whenToUse: When asked for inversion count, similarity between two ranked lists, or 15-puzzle solvability test.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Recommendation engines (Collaborative Filtering preference similarity), Kendall tau distance calculation.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Reduces O(N²) pair comparison to O(N log N) using divide-and-conquer merge sort.

algorithms.title: Pascal's Triangle Algorithm (Combinatorics & Row Generation)
algorithms.summary: Generates Pascal's triangle where each element is the sum of two numbers directly above it.
explanation: Element at row `r` and column `c` (0-indexed) equals combination `nCr(r, c) = r! / (c! * (r - c)!)`.
To generate Row `R` in O(R) time: `val = val * (r - i) / i` iteratively.
To generate full Triangle up to N rows: Maintain 2D array where `row[i][j] = row[i-1][j-1] + row[i-1][j]` with edges = 1.

traceSteps: Generated Row 4 in O(N) time & O(1) auxiliary space: [1, 4, 6, 4, 1].

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Computes binomial coefficients, combinations `nCr`, and probability distribution matrices.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When finding combination values, grid unique paths, or polynomial expansion coefficients.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Binomial distribution calculations, Bezier curve rendering in computer graphics, combinatorics.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Generates Nth row in O(N) time without factorial integer overflow.
